ELLIS ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Properties, LLC · Jordan Lee

PURPOSE OF THIS ELLIS ACT INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's Ellis Act (Government Code sections 7060 through 7060.7), a state statute that prohibits a public entity from compelling the owner of residential real property to offer, or to continue to offer, all of the residential rental units at a property for rent or lease -- in effect permitting a landlord to go out of the residential rental business by withdrawing all of the units from the rental market, subject to notice, tenancy-extension, and re-offering provisions described in this document. It concerns the property commonly known as 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, the landlord Acme Properties, LLC, and the tenancy of Jordan Lee.

This document is distinct from an information sheet describing California's statewide Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (AB 1482), which addresses a different statutory scheme -- a cap on rent increases and a just-cause requirement before ending a tenancy (Civil Code sections 1946.2 and 1947.12). An Ellis Act withdrawal from the rental business is a separate statutory mechanism from that just-cause framework, not a category of just cause defined by it. This document is also distinct from any specific notice of intent to withdraw accommodations that a landlord may deliver to a public entity or to a tenant, and from any specific termination notice, and it describes instead the broader statutory framework within which such notices operate. This information sheet does not itself determine whether any specific structure or unit qualifies as "accommodations" under this chapter, whether the public entity with jurisdiction over 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield has adopted an implementing ordinance or regulation under this chapter, or whether any specific withdrawal, notice, tenancy extension, or re-offering complies with this chapter or with any local ordinance adopted under it.

THE STATEWIDE RIGHT TO WITHDRAW ALL RENTAL UNITS FROM THE MARKET
Government Code section 7060(a) prohibits a public entity from using its statutory, ordinance, regulatory, or administrative power to compel the owner of residential real property to offer, or to continue to offer, "accommodations" in the property for rent or lease, subject to a narrow exception for certain long-standing residential hotels in large cities. Section 7060(b)(1) defines "accommodations" broadly enough to reach an entire property rather than a single unit: for a detached structure with four or more residential rental units, it means the residential rental units in that structure; for a structure with three or fewer residential rental units, it means the residential rental units in that structure and in any other structure on the same parcel of land. Section 7060.7 states that the Legislature's intent in enacting this chapter was to supersede any conflicting holding in Nash v. City of Santa Monica, a California Supreme Court decision, "so as to permit landlords to go out of business." Taken together, these provisions establish the Act's central right: a residential landlord's statutory ability to exit the rental business entirely by withdrawing all of the accommodations at a property from the rental market, notwithstanding a public entity's otherwise-applicable rent-control or eviction-control authority.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "No public entity, as defined in Section 811.2, shall, by statute, ordinance, or regulation, or by administrative action implementing any statute, ordinance or regulation, compel the owner of any residential real property to offer, or to continue to offer, accommodations in the property for rent or lease, except for guestrooms or efficiency units within a residential hotel, as defined in Section 50519 of the Health and Safety Code, if the residential hotel meets all of the following conditions:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 7060(a) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 7060(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7060.)
  "(1) “Accommodations” means either of the following: (A) The residential rental units in any detached physical structure containing four or more residential rental units. (B) With respect to a detached physical structure containing three or fewer residential rental units, the residential rental units in that structure and in any other structure located on the same parcel of land, including any detached physical structure specified in subparagraph (A)."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 7060(b)(1)(A)-(B) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 7060(b)(1)(A)-(B) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7060.)
  "It is the intent of the Legislature in enacting this chapter to supersede any holding or portion of any holding in Nash v. City of Santa Monica, 37 Cal.3d 97 to the extent that the holding, or portion of the holding, conflicts with this chapter, so as to permit landlords to go out of business."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.7 (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 7060.7 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7060.7.)
  Known gap: The citations to Government Code section 7060(a) and section 7060(b)(1) are to subdivisions of the same statutory section; they are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. The citation to section 7060.7 is to a separate, independently numbered section of the same chapter and is offered as independent corroboration of the Legislature's stated purpose. This clause does not reproduce the narrow residential-hotel exception in section 7060(a)(1)-(3) in full, and does not address the *Nash v. City of Santa Monica* decision itself, which this document does not independently verify. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Ellis Act framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific property; a landlord's ability to withdraw rental units from the market, and the conditions on doing so, vary significantly by state. This document addresses California's statewide Ellis Act statute (Government Code sections 7060-7060.7) only. Many California cities and counties with local rent-control or price-control programs -- including San Francisco, Los Angeles, Santa Monica, and West Hollywood, among others -- have adopted their own Ellis Act implementing ordinances or regulations under this chapter, and those local ordinances commonly set their own notice periods, relocation-payment dollar amounts, filing procedures, and re-offering restrictions that go beyond, or fill in gaps left open by, the bare statutory text. This document does not catalog any specific local ordinance, and it does not determine whether any particular public entity has adopted an implementing ordinance or regulation under this chapter. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific structure or unit is "accommodations" within the meaning of this chapter, whether any specific public entity has adopted an implementing statute, ordinance, or regulation under this chapter, whether any specific notice of intent to withdraw complies with this chapter or any local ordinance adopted under it, or whether any specific withdrawal, tenancy extension, or re-offering is lawful.

WITHDRAWAL MUST COVER ALL UNITS, WITH LIMITED OWNER-OCCUPANCY EXCEPTIONS
Government Code section 7060.7 lists things the Ellis Act is "not otherwise intended" to permit, in addition to superseding Nash v. City of Santa Monica. Subdivision (d) states that the Act does not permit an owner to withdraw from rent or lease less than all of the accommodations at a property, as "accommodations" is defined in section 7060(b) -- meaning a landlord's statutory right under this chapter is to withdraw the entire property (or, for a small structure, the entire parcel) from the rental market, not to selectively withdraw only some units while continuing to rent others. Subdivision (d) also states that the Act does not permit an owner to decline to make a written re-rental offer, in the manner and timeframe set out in section 7060.2, to a tenant who occupied a unit when the owner gave notice of intent to withdraw -- except that this re-rental-offer requirement does not apply to a unit that was, and continues to be, the principal residence of the owner or an owner's family member, or to a unit that becomes the owner's own principal residence when the accommodations return to the rental market (subject to a 30-day re-offer obligation if the owner later vacates that unit within 10 years of the withdrawal).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "However, this act is not otherwise intended to do any of the following:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.7 (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 7060.7 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7060.7.)
  "(d) Permit an owner to do any of the following: (1) Withdraw from rent or lease less than all of the accommodations, as defined by paragraph (1) or (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 7060."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.7(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 7060.7(d)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7060.7.)
  "(2) Decline to make a written rerental offer to any tenant or lessee who occupied a unit at the time when the owner gave the public entity notice of its intent to withdraw the accommodations, in the manner and within the timeframe specified in paragraph (3) of subdivision (b), or in subdivision (c), of Section 7060.2. But the requirements of this paragraph shall not apply to: (A) A unit that was the principal place of residence of any owner or owner’s family member at the time of withdrawal, provided that it continues to be that person’s or those persons’ principal place of residence when accommodations are returned to the rental market as provided in this section. (B) A unit that is the principal place of residence of an owner when the accommodations are returned to the rental market, if it is the owners’ principal place of residence, at the time of return to the rental market, as provided in this section. If the owner vacates the unit within 10 years from the date of withdrawal, the owner shall, within 30 days, offer to rerent if required under this paragraph."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.7(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 7060.7(d)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7060.7.)

NOTICE TO THE PUBLIC ENTITY AND THE STATUTORY "DATE OF WITHDRAWAL"
Government Code section 7060.4(a) provides that a public entity that already has some form of price control over rents in effect (adopted as a valid exercise of its police power) may require, by statute, ordinance, or a regulation adopted under section 7060.5, that a landlord file a notice of intent to withdraw accommodations with that entity, and may require that the notice contain sworn statements about the number of units, their address, the tenants' names, and the applicable rents (which the statute treats as confidential information). Section 7060.4(b) provides that, where the public entity's statute, ordinance, or regulation requires the owner to record a summarizing memorandum with the county recorder and to certify that steps to terminate existing tenancies have begun, the statutory "date of withdrawal" of the accommodations -- the trigger date for other deadlines described elsewhere in this chapter -- is 120 days after that notice is delivered to the public entity, in person or by first-class mail. Section 7060.5, a separate section, confirms that a public entity may adopt this notice-and-recording framework either by ordinance or, where its governing body is directly elected, by a form of regulation subject to voter referendum.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) Any public entity which, by a valid exercise of its police power, has in effect any control or system of control on the price at which accommodations are offered for rent or lease, may require by statute or ordinance, or by regulation as specified in Section 7060.5, that the owner notify the entity of an intention to withdraw those accommodations from rent or lease and may require that the notice contain statements, under penalty of perjury, providing information on the number of accommodations, the address or location of those accommodations, the name or names of the tenants or lessees of the accommodations, and the rent applicable to each residential rental unit."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.4(a) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 7060.4(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7060.4.)
  "(b) The statute, ordinance, or regulation of the public entity may require that the owner record with the county recorder a memorandum summarizing the provisions, other than the confidential provisions, of the notice in a form which shall be prescribed by the statute, ordinance, or regulation, and require a certification with that notice that actions have been initiated as required by law to terminate any existing tenancies. In that situation, the date on which the accommodations are withdrawn from rent or lease for purposes of this chapter is 120 days from the delivery in person or by first-class mail of that notice to the public entity."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.4(b) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 7060.4(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7060.4.)
  "The actions authorized by Sections 7060.2 and 7060.4 may be taken by regulation adopted after public notice and hearing by a public body of a public entity, if the members of the body have been elected by the voters of the public entity."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.5 (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 7060.5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7060.5.)

ONE-YEAR EXTENSION FOR A QUALIFYING ELDERLY OR DISABLED TENANT
Within the notice-and-recording framework described elsewhere in this document, Government Code section 7060.4(b) provides an extended timeline for certain tenants: if a tenant or lessee is at least 62 years of age or disabled, and has lived in their unit for at least one year before the date the notice of intent to withdraw was delivered to the public entity, that tenant's own date of withdrawal is extended to one year after that delivery date -- provided the tenant gives the owner written notice of the tenant's entitlement to the extension within 60 days of the notice's delivery to the public entity. During that extended period, the statute requires the tenancy to continue on the same terms and conditions that existed on the date the notice was delivered to the public entity (subject to adjustments otherwise available under the local price-control system), and states that no party is relieved of any obligation under the lease or rental agreement. Section 7060(b)(2), a separate section, defines "disabled" for purposes of this chapter by cross-reference to the definition of disability in Government Code section 12955.3.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "However, if the tenant or lessee is at least 62 years of age or disabled, and has lived in their accommodations or unit within the accommodations for at least one year prior to the date of delivery to the public entity of the notice of intent to withdraw pursuant to subdivision (a), then the date of withdrawal of the accommodations of that tenant or lessee shall be extended to one year after the date of delivery of that notice to the public entity, provided that the tenant or lessee gives written notice of their entitlement to an extension to the owner within 60 days of the date of delivery to the public entity of the notice of intent to withdraw."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.4(b) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 7060.4(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7060.4.)
  "(1) The tenancy shall be continued on the same terms and conditions as existed on the date of delivery to the public entity of the notice of intent to withdraw, subject to any adjustments otherwise available under the system of control. (2) No party shall be relieved of the duty to perform any obligation under the lease or rental agreement."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.4(b)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 7060.4(b)(1)-(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7060.4.)
  "(2) “Disabled” means a person with a disability, as defined in Section 12955.3 of the Government Code."

RESTRICTIONS ON RE-OFFERING WITHDRAWN UNITS, AND THE ABSENCE OF A STATE-SET RELOCATION PAYMENT
Government Code section 7060.2 allows a public entity that already has a rent- or price-control system in effect to provide, by statute, ordinance, or regulation, that units withdrawn under this chapter remain subject to restrictions if they return to the rental market. Under subdivision (b)(3), an owner who offers a unit for rent again must first offer it back to the tenant or lessee displaced from that unit, if that person advised the owner in writing within 30 days of displacement of a desire to be considered for renewal and supplied an address for that purpose; subdivision (b)(1)-(2) separately makes the owner liable to a displaced tenant for actual and exemplary damages, and exposes the owner to a public entity's own suit for exemplary damages, if the unit is re-offered within two years of withdrawal (each within a three-year limitations period). Under subdivision (c), a public entity may extend this first-offer obligation to a period of up to 10 years from withdrawal, with an owner who fails to comply liable for punitive damages up to six months' contract rent. Section 7060.7(d)(2), a separate section, confirms that the Act does not permit an owner to decline to make this written re-rental offer in the manner and timeframe set out in section 7060.2. None of the text of Government Code sections 7060 through 7060.7 sets a specific dollar amount, or a formula for one, that a landlord must pay a displaced tenant as relocation assistance for an Ellis Act withdrawal itself.

  "If a public entity, by valid exercise of its police power, has in effect any control or system of control on the price at which accommodations may be offered for rent or lease, that entity may, notwithstanding any provision of this chapter, provide by statute or ordinance, or by regulation as specified in Section 7060.5, that any accommodations which have been offered for rent or lease and which were subject to that control or system of control at the time the accommodations were withdrawn from rent or lease, shall be subject to the following:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.2 (California Legislative Information text), Gov. C. § 7060.2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7060.2.)

WHAT THE ACT DOES NOT PREEMPT, AND A TENANT'S DEFENSE IN AN UNLAWFUL DETAINER ACTION
Government Code section 7060.1 lists things this chapter does not do, notwithstanding the withdrawal right described in section 7060. Among them, the chapter does not diminish or enhance a public entity's land-use, planning, zoning, or subdivision-map-approval power (except as specifically provided in section 7060.2), and does not diminish or enhance a public entity's power to mitigate the impact of displacement on persons displaced by a withdrawal. Section 7060.1(d) states that the chapter does not supersede several other named bodies of law, including the state relocation-assistance law (Government Code Chapter 16, commencing with section 7260), the Fair Employment and Housing Act (commencing with section 12900), the Unfair Competition Law (Business and Professions Code, commencing with section 17200), a body of Civil Code provisions commencing at section 43, the Mobilehome Residency Law (Civil Code, commencing with section 1925), the state's unlawful detainer procedure (Code of Civil Procedure, commencing with section 1159), and the Community Redevelopment Law (Health and Safety Code, commencing with section 33000). Section 7060.1(e) states that the chapter does not relieve any party to a lease or rental agreement of the duty to perform any obligation under it. Separately, section 7060.6, an independently numbered section, gives a tenant facing an unlawful detainer action arising from an Ellis Act withdrawal the right to appear and answer or demur, and to assert as a defense that the owner has not complied with this chapter or with an implementing statute, ordinance, or regulation adopted under it.

This information sheet describes California's Ellis Act (Government Code sections 7060 through 7060.7), a state statute that prohibits a public entity from compelling the owner of residential real property to offer, or to continue to offer, all of the residential rental units at a property for rent or lease -- in effect permitting a landlord to go out of the residential rental business by withdrawing all of the units from the rental market, subject to notice, tenancy-extension, and re-offering provisions described in this document. It concerns the property commonly known as 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, the landlord Acme Properties, LLC, and the tenancy of Jordan Lee.

This document is distinct from an information sheet describing California's statewide Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (AB 1482), which addresses a different statutory scheme -- a cap on rent increases and a just-cause requirement before ending a tenancy (Civil Code sections 1946.2 and 1947.12). An Ellis Act withdrawal from the rental business is a separate statutory mechanism from that just-cause framework, not a category of just cause defined by it. This document is also distinct from any specific notice of intent to withdraw accommodations that a landlord may deliver to a public entity or to a tenant, and from any specific termination notice, and it describes instead the broader statutory framework within which such notices operate. This information sheet does not itself determine whether any specific structure or unit qualifies as "accommodations" under this chapter, whether the public entity with jurisdiction over 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield has adopted an implementing ordinance or regulation under this chapter, or whether any specific withdrawal, notice, tenancy extension, or re-offering complies with this chapter or with any local ordinance adopted under it.

Government Code section 7060(a) prohibits a public entity from using its statutory, ordinance, regulatory, or administrative power to compel the owner of residential real property to offer, or to continue to offer, "accommodations" in the property for rent or lease, subject to a narrow exception for certain long-standing residential hotels in large cities. Section 7060(b)(1) defines "accommodations" broadly enough to reach an entire property rather than a single unit: for a detached structure with four or more residential rental units, it means the residential rental units in that structure; for a structure with three or fewer residential rental units, it means the residential rental units in that structure and in any other structure on the same parcel of land. Section 7060.7 states that the Legislature's intent in enacting this chapter was to supersede any conflicting holding in Nash v. City of Santa Monica, a California Supreme Court decision, "so as to permit landlords to go out of business." Taken together, these provisions establish the Act's central right: a residential landlord's statutory ability to exit the rental business entirely by withdrawing all of the accommodations at a property from the rental market, notwithstanding a public entity's otherwise-applicable rent-control or eviction-control authority.

expectedJSON.body: Government Code section 7060.7 lists things the Ellis Act is "not otherwise intended" to permit, in addition to superseding Nash v. City of Santa Monica. Subdivision (d) states that the Act does not permit an owner to withdraw from rent or lease less than all of the accommodations at a property, as "accommodations" is defined in section 7060(b) -- meaning a landlord's statutory right under this chapter is to withdraw the entire property (or, for a small structure, the entire parcel) from the rental market, not to selectively withdraw only some units while continuing to rent others. Subdivision (d) also states that the Act does not permit an owner to decline to make a written re-rental offer, in the manner and timeframe set out in section 7060.2, to a tenant who occupied a unit when the owner gave notice of intent to withdraw -- except that this re-rental-offer requirement does not apply to a unit that was, and continues to be, the principal residence of the owner or an owner's family member, or to a unit that becomes the owner's own principal residence when the accommodations return to the rental market (subject to a 30-day re-offer obligation if the owner later vacates that unit within 10 years of the withdrawal).

citations.quote: (e) Relieves any party to a lease or rental agreement of the duty to perform any obligation under that lease or rental agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.6 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If an owner seeks to displace a tenant or lessee from accommodations withdrawn from rent or lease pursuant to this chapter by an unlawful detainer proceeding, the tenant or lessee may appear and answer or demur pursuant to Section 1170 of the Code of Civil Procedure and may assert by way of defense that the owner has not complied with the applicable provisions of this chapter, or statutes, ordinances, or regulations of public entities adopted to implement this chapter, as authorized by this chapter.

expectedJSON.gap: The citations to section 7060.1's lead-in sentence, subdivision (d), and subdivision (e) are to the same statutory section and are treated here as one source. The citation to section 7060.6 is to a separate, independently numbered section and is offered as independent corroboration that this chapter's requirements are judicially enforceable as a defense, not merely aspirational. This clause summarizes, rather than independently verifies the substance of, each of the other statutory schemes that section 7060.1(d) lists as not superseded by this chapter; it does not describe what those other laws themselves require. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Ellis Act framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific property; a landlord's ability to withdraw rental units from the market, and the conditions on doing so, vary significantly by state. This document addresses California's statewide Ellis Act statute (Government Code sections 7060-7060.7) only. Many California cities and counties with local rent-control or price-control programs -- including San Francisco, Los Angeles, Santa Monica, and West Hollywood, among others -- have adopted their own Ellis Act implementing ordinances or regulations under this chapter, and those local ordinances commonly set their own notice periods, relocation-payment dollar amounts, filing procedures, and re-offering restrictions that go beyond, or fill in gaps left open by, the bare statutory text. This document does not catalog any specific local ordinance, and it does not determine whether any particular public entity has adopted an implementing ordinance or regulation under this chapter. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific structure or unit is "accommodations" within the meaning of this chapter, whether any specific public entity has adopted an implementing statute, ordinance, or regulation under this chapter, whether any specific notice of intent to withdraw complies with this chapter or any local ordinance adopted under it, or whether any specific withdrawal, tenancy extension, or re-offering is lawful.
